n: Strengthened by his vision at Bethel, Jacob continues to “the land of the people of the east,” the region of Haran.

f.g: Literally “lifted up his feet”—suggesting renewed energy after Bethel.
Peoples east of Canaan, here the Arameans of Mesopotamia.

n: Jacob comes to a well in a field where three flocks are waiting. A large stone covers the well to protect the precious water.

f.g: Wells are frequent meeting places for future spouses in scripture (24:11; Exodus 2:15-21).

n: The shepherds wait until all the flocks gather, then roll away the heavy stone together, water the sheep, and replace it.

f.g: The stone apparently needed several men to move.

n: Jacob asks where they are from. “Haran,” they say—he has arrived.

f.g: A friendly greeting, “friends.”

n: He asks whether they know Laban, Nahor’s grandson.

f.g: “Son” here means descendant; Laban was Nahor’s grandson (24:29).

n: They say Laban is well—and here comes his daughter Rachel with the sheep. Providence is at work again.

f.g: Literally “Is there peace (shalom) to him?”
Means “ewe”—fitting for a shepherdess.

n: Jacob suggests they water the sheep and send them back to graze, since it is still midday. Perhaps he hopes for privacy with Rachel.

f.g: It is still the middle of the day.

n: The shepherds explain the custom: they wait until all the flocks arrive to move the stone.

f.g: Custom or agreement required them to wait.

n: Rachel arrives with her father’s flock; she is a shepherdess.

f.g: She tended them.

n: Seeing Rachel, Jacob single-handedly rolls the stone away and waters Laban’s flock. His strength and eagerness show his excitement.

f.w: rolled the stone from the well's mouth
f.g: Jacob does alone what normally took several men.

n: Jacob kisses Rachel—a family greeting—and weeps aloud with emotion. After a long, lonely journey, he has found family.

f.g: A customary greeting between relatives.

n: Jacob explains he is her relative, Rebekah’s son. Rachel runs to tell her father.

f.g: Here “brother” means relative; Jacob was Laban’s nephew.

n: Laban runs to meet Jacob, embraces him, and brings him home. He once ran out for Abraham’s servant too—though now Jacob brings no camels laden with gold.
Laban acknowledges Jacob as his own flesh and blood. Jacob stays a month, presumably working for him.

f.g: My own family.

n: Laban offers to pay Jacob, appearing generous—but he is also making Jacob an employee rather than family.

f.g: For nothing; without pay.

n: Laban has two daughters: Leah, the elder, and Rachel, the younger.

f.g: Possibly “cow” or “weary.”

n: Leah had “tender” eyes, while Rachel was beautiful in form and face.

f.g: Hebrew rakkot—soft, delicate, or weak; the meaning is uncertain and may be a compliment.
Good-looking.

n: Jacob loves Rachel and offers seven years of labor as a bride-price, since he has no wealth to give.

f.w: I will serve thee seven years
f.g: A generous offer; bride-prices were often paid in goods.

n: Laban agrees in vague terms—it is better for her to marry family than an outsider.

f.g: Stay with me.

n: Jacob works seven years, and they feel like only a few days because of his love for Rachel. One of the Bible’s most beautiful descriptions of love.

f.w: they seemed unto him but a few days
f.g: Love makes long service feel light.

n: When the seven years end, Jacob asks for his bride.

f.g: My term of service is complete.

n: Laban throws a wedding feast for the whole town.

f.g: A wedding banquet, often with much wine.

n: That evening Laban brings Leah instead of Rachel. In the darkness and with the bride veiled, Jacob does not realize it.

f.g: Darkness and veiling made the switch possible.

n: Laban gives Leah his servant Zilpah as her maid—a customary wedding gift.
Morning reveals Leah. Jacob protests that he was deceived. The deceiver has been deceived—the elder substituted for the younger, just as Jacob once posed as the elder.

f.g: Deceived; tricked.

n: Laban claims local custom: the younger daughter cannot marry before the firstborn. His words sting, given Jacob’s own history with the firstborn’s rights.

f.g: Laban’s word choice echoes Jacob’s deception of his father.

n: Laban offers Rachel too after the week-long wedding celebration—if Jacob works seven more years.

f.g: Complete the seven-day wedding celebration with Leah.

n: Jacob agrees, finishes the week, and marries Rachel as well.

f.g: Jacob now has two wives who are sisters—later forbidden in the law of Moses (Leviticus 18:18).

n: Laban gives Rachel his servant Bilhah as her maid.
Jacob loves Rachel more than Leah and serves seven more years. Favoritism again sows trouble in the family.

f.w: loved also Rachel more than Leah
f.g: The family pattern of favoritism continues (25:28; 37:3).

n: The Lord sees that Leah is unloved and opens her womb, while Rachel remains childless. God notices and cares for the overlooked.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom meaning “loved less,” not necessarily active hatred.

n: Leah names her first son Reuben, hoping her husband will now love her. Each name reveals the ache of her heart.

f.g: Sounds like “See, a son!” and “the LORD has seen my affliction.”

n: Her second son is Simeon, because the Lord “heard” she was unloved.

f.g: From Hebrew shamaʿ, “to hear.”

n: Her third son is Levi, hoping her husband will now be “joined” to her. Levi’s descendants will become Israel’s priestly tribe.

f.g: Sounds like Hebrew lawah, “joined” or “attached.”

n: With her fourth son, Leah’s focus shifts: “Now will I praise the LORD.” She names him Judah. From Judah come King David and Jesus Christ.

f.g: Related to Hebrew yadah, “to praise.”
